question: Which of the following best explains why ₹1,000 today is worth more than ₹1,000 a year from now?
before: Opportunity cost is the primary driver of TVM — money available today can be invested to earn returns. A is backward (prices increase). C is made up. D is too narrow; TVM applies even without banks.
after:
Concept: Time value of money (TVM) rests on the principle that a rupee today is worth more than the same rupee in the future because today's rupee can be invested to generate additional returns over that time period.

Why this is correct: Option B identifies opportunity cost as the fundamental reason. Money in hand today has the potential to earn returns through investment—whether in bank deposits, bonds, equities, or other assets. This earning potential makes present money more valuable than future money. This is the core principle underpinning all TVM calculations in finance.

Why the others are wrong:

A) Assumes prices decrease over time, which contradicts economic reality. Inflation causes prices to rise, making future rupees less able to buy the same goods—but this is a consequence of TVM, not the cause. TVM applies even in a zero-inflation scenario.

C) No government guarantee determines the value of money over time. The concept applies universally to all entities and scenarios, not just those with government backing.

D) While bank interest is one example of earning returns on money, it is too narrow. TVM exists independently of banking systems. An investor could earn returns through business investment, equity markets, or lending to others. The principle applies whether or not banks are involved.

Intuition: In equity research, recognizing opportunity cost is critical when valuing a company's cash position or discounting future cash flows. Money sitting idle today represents foregone returns that shareholders could have earned elsewhere, which is why future cash flows must be discounted back to present value at a rate reflecting that opportunity cost. This concept underpins discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis, the foundation of fundamental equity valuation.
